background.definition: Leprosy, known as Hansen's disease (HD), is a chronic granulomatous disease primarily affecting the peripheral nerves and skin; it is caused by Mycobacterium leprae. Two forms exist: lepromatous (LHD) and tuberculoid (THD), with the latter having fewer dermatologic manifestations. Borderline leprosy (BHD) is neither as strictly localized as THD nor as diffuse as LHD. Indeterminate leprosy (IHD) is an early phase of the disease that is not yet differentiated into LHD or THD. Histoid leprosy (HHD) is a rare variant of LHD in which bacteria-rich dome-shaped nodules arise from normal-appearing skin.

list.listitem: Worldwide case detection rate (per million population) ranges from <0.1 in Europe to 70.4 in Southeast Asia; in the Americas, it is 29.5.
In the United States, most cases are in immigrants, but there is an endemic region in Texas with an average incidence of approximately 2 cases per million population.
Worldwide, 63% of cases are among males and 11% are pediatric cases.
Incidence rate of leprosy among contacts of leprosy patients is 0.017 cases/person-year.
Leprosy is a leading communicable cause of permanent physical disability. It is disfiguring and carries a heavy social stigma.

Worldwide prevalence was 133,802 cases (0.17 per 10,000 population) in 2021, down from over 5,000,000 in the 1980s. In the United States, more than 100 new cases are reported per year, primarily in immigrants.
The disease affects mainly young adults in their most productive stage of life.
Studies of disability-adjusted work life years (DAWLYs) in patients with leprosy indicate a lost of nearly 14 years of productive working life.

Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular, acid-fast bacillus. Another organism, M. lepromatosis, is a recently identified, molecularly unique variant which causes an indistinguishable clinical disease.

No association of index cases with HIV disease, nutrition, socioeconomic status, or occupation. Leprosy in contacts, however, is associated with social determinants of health including age, income, and education level.
Though primarily transmitted human-to-human, extra-human reservoirs of M. leprae exist, hampering eradication efforts.

There are strong genetic determinants of susceptibility; with 95% of humans naturally resistant to the organism, some have suggested leprosy is primarily a genetic disease rather than an infectious one.
A systematic review identified 10 cases of Hansen's disease emerging after treatment with a TNF-alpha inhibitor such as infliximab.

The portal of entry is not certain but is widely believed to be upper respiratory tract primarily and broken skin to a lesser degree. The organism is found in nasal and sebaceous secretions of infected individuals.
The incubation period is generally between 3 and 5 years, but it may be decades in some cases.
Bacilli infiltrate the skin and enter nerves, multiplying within Schwann cells and histiocytes. Other tissues are also affected (see ).
Nerve involvement results in loss of both sensory and motor function, with the former predominant. Vibratory and proprioception may be preserved.

Microbiologic isolates do not vary in virulence; host immune response determines the course of the disease. LHD is due to a humoral-mediated host response; THD represents the pathology resulting from the host's cell-mediated response.
HHD may represent a significant reservoir of infection of drug resistant strains.
Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination offers some protection. B
Leprosy-specific vaccination appears to be effective, although it is not yet widely available even abroad. B

Chemoprophylaxis using rifampicin 600 mg in a single dose is effective when used with household contacts; dapsone is another option (see ).A However, this is somewhat controvertial from an antibiotic stewardship perspective. More effective post-exposure prophylaxis regiments, PEP++, are being developed.

A study in Madagascar used rifampicin at higher dose (20mg/kg) looking at treatment of household contacts, near neighbors, and no-treatment controls. It enrolled 109,436 patients and demonstrated a reduction of spread, with an incidence rate ratio (IRR) of 0.56 (p=0.0030) among household contacts and IRR of 0.55 (p=0.0050) including both household contacts and those living within 100 m of the index case. The authors concluded that single dose rifampacin is effective, though less than anticipated.

A large cluster randomized trial in China randomized 68 clusters (2331 household contacts 10 and older) to a single dose of rifapentine 600 mg, 71 clusters (2760 contacts) to rifampin 600 mg, and 68 clusters (2359 contacts) to no-treatment controls. After 4 years, incidence of leprosy in household contacts was 0.09% in the rifapentine group, 0.33% in the rifampin group, and 0.55% in the no treatment group. Rifapentine was significantly better than no treatment but not rifampin (cumulative incidence ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.57).

Efforts at early identification of infection in household contacts through molecular methods have been disappointing: detection of M. leprae DNA does not predict development of infection or clinical disease in these individuals.

list.listitem: Defined by WHO as having one or more of the following and having yet to complete the full course of treatment: (1) hypopigmented or reddish skin lesions with definite loss of sensation, (2) involvement of peripheral nerves as demonstrated by definite thickening with loss of sensation, or (3) skin smear positive for acid-fast bacilli.
WHO recognizes three types of cases: pausibacillary single lesion (PB-1); pausibacillary (PB) (2-5 lesions); and multibacillary (MB) (>5 lesions). 69% of casess are multibacillary.
Diagnosis is conclusive if Kinyoun-negative acid-fast bacilli are found in nerves or foamy histiocytes on pathologic section, but the correlation between clinical diagnosis and histopathology is low.
Insidious onset is usual, although rarely an acute presentation may be seen.
Pale or red patches on skin are the most common sign, accompanied by loss of feeling in the patch. This is present in 70% of HD patients, primarily those with the multibacillary form of the disease.
Numbness/tingling of extremities, painless wounds, and weakness of hands, feet, and eyelids may be present but are also seen in other conditions.
Thickened peripheral nerves are seen, and they may be painful.
Neurologic findings in the absence of dermatologic findings may be seen in THD but not in LHD. Skin findings are present in 90% of cases; 10% exhibit neurological deficits alone.
Treatment of rheumatological conditions by pharmacological immunosuppression, especially with biologics, has been associated with increased risk of developing or reactivating leprosy.
Diagnosis is usually made clinically. Confirmation is demonstration of the bacilli by histologic or molecular studies.
The confirmatory study recommended by WHO is the slit-skin smear. Of these smears, 70% are negative for the bacilli, but if positive can be used to monitor treatment.
Histology of biopsy may be supportive but is only confirmatory if acid-fast bacilli are identified. They may be seen in LHD but usually not in THD or IHD.
Dot-ELISA of skin scraping has a reported sensitivity of 62% to 76% in PB HD, with 100% in MB HD.

Augumented intelligence (AI) in the histopathological diagnosis of leprosy shows a sensitivity of 74% and specificity of 65% (overall accuracy 70%), and may emerge as a viable tool in high-resource settings.

Both serological and molecular detection methods detect evidence of the organism is a fair number of asymptomatic individuals—both close contacts of leprosy patients and the general population in endemic areas—yet few go on to develop disease.

Molecular studies are of debatable clinical value: molecular probes of biopsies may miss PB cases, and while polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can detect even one organism, it also detects nonviable organisms so is not useful to monitor treatment. Whole-blood nested-PCR shows promise in preliminary studies.
Blood transciption marker levels (RISK4LEP) can predict clinical leprosy from 4 months to 5 years prior to symtom onset and are an emerging diagnostic tool.

Serology is less valuable for initial diagnosis; it is mainly helpful in monitoring treatment and disease progression. Fluorescent leprosy antibody absorption (FLA-ABS) assesses humoral response; lepromin assesses cell-mediated immunity.
Dermatoscopy demonstrates novel findings that provide a rapid, noninvasive method that can aid in diagnosis and differntiation of leprosy types.
Advanced imaging of the central nervous system (CNS) should be considered for cranial nerve palsies; leprosy may affect the central nervous system, though less commonly than peripheral nerves.
A clinical prediction rule has been developed and validated to predict the likelihood of nerve function impairment in patients with HD.
In patients with paucibacillary disease, the risk is 1.3% if no nerve impairment exists on presentation and 16% if there is nerve impairment on presentation.
In patients with multibacillary disease, the risk is 16% if no nerve impairment exists on presentation and 65% if there is nerve impairment on presentation.

Examine all skin in good light; note the number of patches, test for loss of sensation in patches, and assess disability. (WHO grades disability as follows: 0 = no disability, 1 = loss of sensation, and 2 = visible damage or disability.)

Evaluate for nerve enlargement. The most commonly affected nerves are the great auricular, ulnar, radial cutaneous, median, common peroneal, and posterior tibial. Test sensation and motor strength ().
Confirm clinical diagnosis via bacteriologic studies (biopsy or immunologic or molecular techniques).
Multidrug therapy (MDT) is needed. B
Bedaquiline is a drug that can be used as monotherapy but is still in clinical trials.B
Tolerance of treatment may be a problem. B
Except in the case of severe (Type I or Type II) reactions, steroids offer no significant benefit. B
Severe reactions, severe disability, and eye involvement may require referral. C
Immunotherapy may have a role as an adjunct to chemotherapy in high bacterial index cases of LHD. B
Usual first-line treatment is long-term multidrug therapy with dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine:
Previously, treatment recommendations were relatively standardized; in 2018 new WHO guidelines were released which diverge from the USA regimens () Dosing for children is on .
A recent meta-analysis suggests the addition of perfloxacin or ofloxacin can augment the efficacy of the WHO MDT regimen.

Bedaquiline is a diarylquinoline which inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase. It was evaluated in a Phase 2 uncontrolled series 11 patients in Brazil. They received 200 mg once daily for 2 weeks, and then 100 mg orally three times per week for 6 additional weeks. After 4 weeks all patients had gone from 100% showing positive M. leprae growth to 0%. Skin lesion appearance also improved.

Though antileprosy drugs cross the placenta and are excreted in breast milk, multidrug therapy for leprosy patients should be administered in pregnancy and lactation. The only reported adverse affect on the child is possible skin discoloration due to clofazimine.

For national leprosy programs, a uniform multidrug therapy regimen ("U-MDT") employing rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for 6 months for both PB and MB has been demonstrated to be both effective and reasonably well-tolerated. B

Treatment is often not well tolerated, with side effects in 45%, severe enough to result in withdrawal of treatment in 24%. Dapsone hypersensitivity reactions are associated with a 9.9% fatality rate.
Drug resistance to first-line agents is an increasing problem.

In cases of patient intolerance to, or treatment failure with, the first-line agents, second-line treatment includes the combination of clarithromycin, a fluoroquinolone, and minocycline. In cases of rifampicin-resistance, this alternative regimen must be administered daily for 24 months. The specific combination depends on the agent to which the patient is intolerant—see link to WHO Technical Report Series, below in "Additional Resources" section, for direction.

A proposed shorter course option (rifampicin, sparfloxacin, minocycline, and clarithromycin for 12 weeks) has not been endorsed by WHO. Formerly, WHO recommended a single-dose combination of rifampicin, ofloxacin and minocycline for PB-1, but withdrew this recommendation in 2012.
Moderate quality evidence shows minimal to no benefit with steroids to improve symptoms from nerve damage. However, a recent meta-analysis suggests prednisolone may augment MDT efficacy.
Topically applied granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor demonstrates some potential to accelerate the healing of leprous ulcers.

Decompressive surgery has been recommended for treating nerve damage. However, a systematic review identified only two RCTs with 88 participants, and found no significant difference between surgical and non-surgical groups.
Severe reactions, severe secondary infections, and serious drug reactions require inpatient care.
Eye involvement requires urgent ophthalmologic consultation.
Disabilities suitable for surgical remediation require referral.
Suspected relapse or resistant infection.
Many leprosy pateints first encounter the medical system "in reaction". Three types of reactions may be seen:

Type I: Type I, known as "Lepra", "upgrading reaction", or "reversal reactions," are cell mediated, type IV hypersensitivity reactions in which the leprosy lesions become inflamed. Mechanisms include molecular mimicry, autophagy, and T-cell and B-cell alterations. Lepra reaction is rare in HHD. A Type I reaction is the only true emergency in leprosy, especially when there is weakness and swelling of motor nerves. Treatment of Type I reactions is prednisone 60 to 80mg daily.

Type II: Type II, or erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), are Coombs type III reactions with vasculitis in which the leprosy lesions themselves remain unchanged, but new inflammatory nodules appear. Neutrophils play a key role, and both T-cells and B-cells are altered. Iritis and orchitis may develop. Standard treatment is thalidomide 400mg daily with the possible addition of steroids.
Lucio Reaction: Severe vasculitis, which is also called a Lucio reaction, results in vascular occlusion that produces symmetric necrotic lesions.

Severe leprosy reactions (type I or II) may benefit from 3 to 6 months of steroids, although clinical trial data is limited. A systematic review of treatments for ENL found small trials showing no differences for comparisons of betamethasone vs dextrose, pentoxifyllin vs thalidomide, levamisole vs placebo, and indomethacin vs prednisolone, aspirin, or chloroquine. There was an increased likelihood of remission with thalidomide (RR 2.4; 95% CI 1.3-4.6) when compared with aspirin. However, a systematic review found inadequate evidence to support for the efficacy of thalidomide or chlofazimine in the treatment of ENL. Case reports suggest that TNFα-inhibitors may be effective for refractory ENL.
Eye involvement requires ophthalmologic care.
Facial deformities may benefit from plastic surgery.
Arthropathies associated with leprosy may benefit from the addition of biologics or synthetic antiinflamatories to the multidrug therapy.
Aggressive physical and occupational therapy can minimize disability.
Psychosocial complications may benefit from counseling, and socioeconomic interventions have demonstrated some benefit in overcoming stigma associated the disease.
Multidrug treatment is effective at eliminating infection; early detection and treatment is effective at preventing disability. B
Follow-up recommendations depend on the risk of developing nerve impairment.B
Most "cases" are asymptomatic but do show laboratory evidence of infection (colonization?).
Of those developing clinical disease, THD is predominant.
Spontaneous recovery is common, but some patients go on to develop disability and disfigurement if untreated.
Spontaneous recovery of nerve function is a common phenomenon, especially mild nerve impairment.
With proper rehabilitation, deformities and disability can be largely prevented or corrected.
Multi-drug treatment is effective at eliminating infection; early detection and treatment are effective at preventing disability.
Microbiological relapse rate after 12 month multi-drug treatment for MB is 1.7%.
Neuropathic pain, often associated with significant psychological depression, is common in treated patients.

Degree of impairment at time of diagnosis is a strong predictor of neurological worsening after receiving proper treatment. Early diagnosis and treatment decreases the likelihood of long-term disability.
Timing of follow-up depends on the risk of developing nerve impairment. B
PB with no impairment: barring new symptoms, needs no follow-up upon completion of treatment.
PB with impairment and MB with no impairment: need regular monitoring for at least 12 months.
MB with impairment: requires a minimum of 24 months of monitoring.
Several tools are available to monitor improvement.
The Impairment Summary Form is sensitive enough (90%) to aid in clinical decision making (see ). B
The Eye, Hand, and Foot Impairment Score is better for program monitoring than for individual monitoring (61% sensitivity).
The Maximum WHO Impairment Grade should be limited to an indicator of late case detection (sensitivity 88%).
Reassure patients that HD is curable and that they can expect to live a normal life following treatment.
Instruct patients with nerve damage about prevention-of-disability activities.
Physical and occupational therapy are essential components of treatment.
Pregnancy increases the risk of acquiring HD. HD also may become worse in pregnancy; pregnancy may precipitate ENL and may prompt relapse of HD. HD is also associated with low birth weight infants.
Postpartum patients may be at higher risk for type I (but not ENL) reactions and neuritis.

Though antileprosy drugs cross the placenta and are excreted in breast milk, multidrug therapy for leprosy patients should be administered in pregnancy and lactation. The only reported adverse affect on the child is possible skin discoloration due to clofazimine.
HD has no effect on female fertility, but LHD can cause male sterility.
Very short incubation periods have been reported for infants developing leprosy.
